chunks: And from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Gabriel descended upon the Prophet (peace be upon him) and said: O Muhammad, your Lord says: One who humiliates My believing servant has confronted Me with war.

And My believing servant draws closer to Me with nothing better than fulfilling the obligatory acts; and indeed, he performs supererogatory acts for Me until I love him. So, when I love him, I become his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he grasps, and his leg with which he walks.
And I did not hesitate in anything that I am to do as I hesitate in the death of My believing servant; he experiences death and I dislike his suffering.

And among the believers there are some who will not be well except by destitution, and if I were to surround them with wealth, it would be evil for them; and among them are some who are not well except in affluence, and if I were to surround them with poverty, it would be evil for them.
And indeed, My servant asks Me to fulfill a need, but I deny him that because of what is best for him.
ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual significance of a believer's obligatory and supererogatory acts in Shia theology?
ai.summary: This hadith qudsi, recorded in *Kitab al-Mumin*, elucidates the metaphysical elevation of the believer (*al-mu'min*) through divine intimacy, where obligatory acts (*fara'id*) serve as the foundation for God's transformation of the servant's faculties. It further contextualizes divine decree (*qada'*) by illustrating that poverty or wealth are not absolute goods but are dispensed with wisdom to ensure the believer's ultimate spiritual benefit, a concept central to Shia theological reflections on *hikmah* (divine wisdom).
